Find the nth Prime Number

nthPrime.Rd

Find the prime number at a given position in the increasing sequence of primes. Positions start at 1, so the first prime is 2.

Usage

nthPrime(n, nThreads = NULL)

Arguments

n

A single positive whole number, at most 252,252,704,148,404. This is the position of the prime to find, not an upper bound on the prime's value.

nThreads

Requested number of threads. The default is NULL for serial execution. Requests are capped by the available hardware and the useful work in the calculation. Small or simple cases may use fewer threads. This argument is validated even when the result is immediate.

Details

Let \(p_n\) denote the \(n\)th prime. The result is the unique integer \(p_n\) satisfying $$\pi(p_n - 1) = n - 1, \qquad \pi(p_n) = n,$$ where \(\pi(x)\) counts the primes less than or equal to \(x\). For example, nthPrime(25) returns 97, whereas primeCount(25) returns 9.

Small positions use a lookup table. Otherwise, the calculation starts with an approximation to \(p_n\), obtains an exact prime count at that location, and finishes with a segmented sieve. At most one additional whole-range prime count is used. Counts over nearby intervals may then refine the search location without recounting all preceding primes. Approximation errors affect the amount of work, not the correctness of the result: the sieve continues until it finds the required prime.

The whole-range counts use Legendre, Meissel, or Lehmer, with the same size and thread thresholds used to choose among those methods in primeCount. Prepared prime and prime-count tables are reused for these counts, then released before interval sieving. Simple size bands, based on the search location rather than the requested position, determine when to switch to sieving. Interval counting and final selection reuse the same sieve as primeSieve. Requested threads apply to both counting and sieving, subject to the useful work available.

The largest supported position is \(\pi(2^{53} - 1)\), so the returned prime is at most \(2^{53} - 1\) and is represented exactly. The table memory grows with the square root of the search location. Near the upper limit, the dense prime-count table alone occupies about 362 MiB, in addition to the prime vector, shared Phi cache, and worker storage. Final selection retains generated primes from a window of at most one million integer positions at a time. Interval counting retains no generated prime values; both sieve stages also require base-prime and worker storage.

Logical inputs TRUE are converted to 1. Missing values, FALSE, non-finite values, fractional values, and vectors of length other than 1 are not supported. nThreads = NULL is supported as described above.

Value

A single prime number. The result is of type integer when it is at most .Machine$integer.max, and numeric otherwise.

See also

primeCount, primeSieve, isPrimeRcpp

References

Axler, C. (2018). New estimates for the nth prime number. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03651

Walisch, K. primecount: prime counting and nth-prime algorithms. https://github.com/kimwalisch/primecount

Examples

nthPrime(1)
#> [1] 2
nthPrime(25)
#> [1] 97
nthPrime(1000000)
#> [1] 15485863

## The result has exactly n primes at or below it
n <- 1000
p <- nthPrime(n)
primeCount(p)
#> [1] 1000
primeCount(p - 1)
#> [1] 999

## Use multiple threads for counting and sieving when useful
nthPrime(1000000, nThreads = 2)
#> [1] 15485863
